records.source: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא נָתַ֞ן הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ֙ לְאֶסְתֵּ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה אֶת־בֵּ֥ית הָמָ֖ן צֹרֵ֣ר הַיְּהוּדִ֑ים וּמָרְדֳּכַ֗י בָּ֚א לִפְנֵ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ כִּֽי־הִגִּ֥ידָה אֶסְתֵּ֖ר מַ֥ה הוּא־לָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: On the day the that gave the king Ahasuerus to Esther the queen the house of Haman, [the] harasser of the Jews, and Mordecai came before the king, for had told Esther what he [was] to her.
pieces: That same day King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther the estate of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. And Mordecai came into the king's presence, because Esther had told how he was related to her.

L.1: On that day King Ahasuerus gave to Esther the queen the house of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. And Mordecai came before the king, for Esther had told what he was to her.

R.1: That same day King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther everything that had belonged to Haman, the enemy of the Jews. Mordecai came to see the king, because Esther had told the king that Mordecai was her cousin and had raised her.

decisions.choice: the house of Haman: his household and property
decisions.reason: "House" here means everything Haman owned, his estate and household. The condemned man's goods pass to the king, and the king gives them to the queen whose people Haman tried to destroy.

decisions.choice: the harasser of the Jews: the enemy of the Jews
decisions.reason: The word means one who shows hostility, an adversary. It is Haman's title in the book (3:10; 9:10, 24).

decisions.choice: what he was to her: Mordecai was her cousin who had raised her
decisions.reason: Mordecai was the son of Esther's uncle and had brought her up as his own daughter after her parents died (2:7, 15). Esther had kept this secret on his orders (2:10, 20); now she tells the king.

decisions.choice: estate; everything that had belonged to Haman
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "house" means here; Literal keeps "house".

decisions.choice: that Mordecai was her cousin and had raised her
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the relationship from 2:7.

records.heading: Mordecai receives the king's signet ring

records.source: וַיָּ֨סַר הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ אֶת־טַבַּעְתּ֗וֹ אֲשֶׁ֤ר הֶֽעֱבִיר֙ מֵֽהָמָ֔ן וַֽיִּתְּנָ֖הּ לְמָרְדֳּכָ֑י וַתָּ֧שֶׂם אֶסְתֵּ֛ר אֶֽת־מָרְדֳּכַ֖י עַל־בֵּ֥ית הָמָֽן׃פ
records.gloss: And removed the king his signet ring that he had taken away from Haman and gave it to Mordecai. And set Esther Mordecai over [the] house of Haman.
pieces: The king took off his signet ring, which he had taken back from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. And Esther put Mordecai in charge of Haman's estate.

L.2: And the king took off his signet ring, which he had taken away from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. And Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman.

R.2: The king took off his signet ring, the one he had taken back from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. Esther put Mordecai in charge of everything Haman had owned.

decisions.choice: the signet ring: the power to seal orders in the king's name
decisions.reason: Whoever held the king's seal could issue orders with his authority. The king had given it to Haman to seal the decree against the Jews (3:10, 12); now it goes to Mordecai, who takes Haman's place (compare Genesis 41:42).

decisions.choice: Esther set Mordecai over the house: she makes him manager of the estate
decisions.reason: The estate belongs to Esther (verse 1), and she appoints Mordecai to run it. Mordecai now holds both Haman's office and his property.

decisions.choice: estate; everything Haman had owned
decisions.reason: As in verse 1, Balanced and Readable say what "house" means.

records.source: וַתּ֣וֹסֶף אֶסְתֵּ֗ר וַתְּדַבֵּר֙ לִפְנֵ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַתִּפֹּ֖ל לִפְנֵ֣י רַגְלָ֑יו וַתֵּ֣בְךְּ וַתִּתְחַנֶּן־ל֗וֹ לְהַֽעֲבִיר֙ אֶת־רָעַת֙ הָמָ֣ן הָֽאֲגָגִ֔י וְאֵת֙ מַֽחֲשַׁבְתּ֔וֹ אֲשֶׁ֥ר חָשַׁ֖ב עַל־הַיְּהוּדִֽים׃
records.gloss: And again Esther spoke before the king, and she fell before his feet and wept and sought favor from him to take away [the] evil of Haman the Agagite and his scheme that he had schemed against the Jews.
pieces: Esther spoke to the king once more. She fell at his feet, weeping, and begged him to undo the evil of Haman the Agagite, the scheme he had devised against the Jews.

L.3: And Esther spoke again before the king, and she fell before his feet and wept and pleaded with him to take away the evil of Haman the Agagite and his scheme that he had devised against the Jews.

R.3: Once again Esther went to speak to the king. She threw herself down at his feet and cried. She begged him to stop the evil plan that Haman the Agagite had made against the Jews.

decisions.choice: Haman is dead, but his scheme still stands
decisions.reason: Haman has been hanged, but the decree sealed in the king's name to destroy the Jews on the thirteenth of Adar is still in force (3:12-13). Esther's second plea is for that decree to be undone.

decisions.choice: falling at his feet, weeping and pleading: an urgent, humble appeal
decisions.reason: Throwing oneself at a ruler's feet was the posture of someone begging for mercy (1 Samuel 25:23-24; 2 Kings 4:37). Esther, already queen and favored, still comes as a petitioner.

decisions.choice: take away: cause to pass, avert
decisions.reason: The same verb was used in verse 2 for the ring the king "took away" from Haman. Esther asks the king to take away Haman's evil plan as he took away Haman's ring.

decisions.choice: the Agagite
decisions.reason: Haman's title recalls Agag, king of Amalek, Israel's old enemy (1 Samuel 15; see 3:1). The book does not explain it, and it is a link the text invites rather than states.

decisions.choice: undo
decisions.reason: Balanced uses "undo" for "take away", since Esther asks for the plan to be reversed.

records.heading: Esther pleads again for her people

records.source: וַיּ֤וֹשֶׁט הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ לְאֶסְתֵּ֔ר אֵ֖ת שַׁרְבִ֣ט הַזָּהָ֑ב וַתָּ֣קָם אֶסְתֵּ֔ר וַֽתַּעֲמֹ֖ד לִפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And held out the king to Esther the scepter of the gold, and arose Esther and stood before the king.
pieces: The king held out the golden scepter to Esther, and she rose and stood before the king.

L.4: And the king held out to Esther the scepter of gold, and Esther rose and stood before the king.

R.4: The king held out his gold scepter to Esther. So she got up and stood in front of him.

decisions.choice: the golden scepter: a sign of the king's favor
decisions.reason: Anyone who came to the king without being called could be put to death unless he held out his golden scepter (4:11; 5:2). Here the gesture accepts Esther's plea and invites her to rise and speak. The text does not say whether she had come uncalled again.

decisions.choice: she arose and stood: from lying at his feet to standing before him
decisions.reason: Esther rises from where she had fallen (verse 3) and now stands to make her request formally.

records.source: וַ֠תֹּאמֶר אִם־עַל־הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ ט֜וֹב וְאִם־מָצָ֧אתִי חֵ֣ן לְפָנָ֗יו וְכָשֵׁ֤ר הַדָּבָר֙ לִפְנֵ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְטוֹבָ֥ה אֲנִ֖י בְּעֵינָ֑יו יִכָּתֵ֞ב לְהָשִׁ֣יב אֶת־הַסְּפָרִ֗ים מַחֲשֶׁ֜בֶת הָמָ֤ן בֶּֽן־הַמְּדָ֨תָא֙ הָאֲגָגִ֔י אֲשֶׁ֣ר כָּתַ֗ב לְאַבֵּד֙ אֶת־הַיְּהוּדִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֖ר בְּכָל־מְדִינ֥וֹת הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And she said, If on the king [it is] good, and if I have found favor before him, and right [is] the matter before the king, and good I [am] in his eyes, let it be written to turn back the letters, [the] scheme of Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, which he wrote to destroy the Jews who [are] in all [the] provinces of the king.
pieces: She said, "If it pleases the king, and if I have found favor with him, and if the matter seems right to the king, and if I am pleasing to him, let an order be written to revoke the letters devised by Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, which he wrote to destroy the Jews in all the king's provinces.

L.5: And she said, "If it is good to the king, and if I have found favor before him, and the matter is right before the king, and I am pleasing in his eyes, let it be written to revoke the letters, the scheme of Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, which he wrote to destroy the Jews who are in all the provinces of the king.

R.5: She said, "Your Majesty, if it pleases you, and if you are pleased with me, and if you think this is right, and if you are happy with me, please write an order to cancel the letters that Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite sent out. His plan was to destroy the Jews in all your provinces.

decisions.choice: four conditions: a carefully courteous request
decisions.reason: Esther stacks four "if" clauses, two about the king's judgment and two about his favor toward her, before she makes her request. It is the most elaborate courtesy she uses in the book.

decisions.choice: turn back the letters: revoke the decree
decisions.reason: The verb means to turn back or cancel. But a decree written in the king's name and sealed with his ring could not be revoked (1:19; 8:8), so the king will answer by allowing a second decree instead.

decisions.choice: the scheme of Haman, which he wrote: Esther lays the blame on Haman
decisions.reason: Esther speaks of the letters as Haman's scheme and Haman's writing, not the king's, though they were sent in the king's name and sealed with his ring (3:12). This lets the king change course without being blamed.

decisions.choice: Your Majesty, ... you
decisions.reason: Readable lets Esther address the king directly as "you", since the third-person court style ("the king", "him") could confuse a new reader.

records.source: כִּ֠י אֵיכָכָ֤ה אוּכַל֙ וְֽרָאִ֔יתִי בָּרָעָ֖ה אֲשֶׁר־יִמְצָ֣א אֶת־עַמִּ֑י וְאֵֽיכָכָ֤ה אוּכַל֙ וְֽרָאִ֔יתִי בְּאָבְדַ֖ן מוֹלַדְתִּֽי׃ס
records.gloss: For how will I be able and look on the evil that will find my people, and how will I be able and look on [the] destruction of my kindred?
pieces: For how can I bear to see the disaster that is coming on my people? How can I bear to see my family destroyed?"

L.6: For how can I bear to look on the evil that will find my people? And how can I bear to look on the destruction of my kindred?"

R.6: How could I stand to watch this disaster happen to my people? How could I stand to see my own relatives killed?"

decisions.choice: two parallel questions: I cannot bear it
decisions.reason: The two questions say the same thing twice for force. They are not real questions but a cry that she cannot watch her people die.

decisions.choice: my kindred: my family and the people I was born into
decisions.reason: The word means one's relatives and birth-family, the very thing Esther had concealed (2:10, 20). It stands in parallel with "my people".

decisions.choice: bear to look on; bear to see; stand to watch
decisions.reason: "How can I ... and look" means "how could I endure seeing"; every level adds "bear" or "stand" to say so.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֹשׁ֙ לְאֶסְתֵּ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה וּֽלְמָרְדֳּכַ֖י הַיְּהוּדִ֑י הִנֵּ֨ה בֵית־הָמָ֜ן נָתַ֣תִּי לְאֶסְתֵּ֗ר וְאֹתוֹ֙ תָּל֣וּ עַל־הָעֵ֔ץ עַ֛ל אֲשֶׁר־שָׁלַ֥ח יָד֖וֹ בַּיְּהוּדִֽים׃
records.gloss: And said the king Ahasuerus to Esther the queen and to Mordecai the Jew, Look, [the] house of Haman I have given to Esther, and him they have hanged on the tree, because he sent his hand against the Jews.
pieces: King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, "Look, I have given Haman's estate to Esther, and he has been hanged on the gallows because he tried to attack the Jews.

L.7: And King Ahasuerus said to Esther the queen and to Mordecai the Jew, "Look, the house of Haman I have given to Esther, and him they have hanged on the gallows, because he stretched out his hand against the Jews.

R.7: King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and Mordecai the Jew, "Look, I have given Haman's property to Esther, and Haman has been hanged on the gallows because he tried to destroy the Jews.

decisions.choice: look what I have done: the king points to what he has already given
decisions.reason: The king begins with what he has already done for Esther and the Jews. He does not cancel the first decree, which he cannot do (verse 8), but shows his goodwill before giving them power to write a new one.

decisions.choice: sent his hand against the Jews: tried to destroy them
decisions.reason: To "send one's hand against" means to attack (see 6:2). The king now names Haman's plot against the Jews as the reason for his death; in 7:8-9 the charges were an assault on the queen and the gallows meant for Mordecai.

decisions.choice: tried to attack; tried to destroy
decisions.reason: Haman's attack was planned but not carried out, so Balanced and Readable say "tried".

records.heading: A new decree written to every province

records.source: וְ֠אַתֶּם כִּתְב֨וּ עַל־הַיְּהוּדִ֜ים כַּטּ֤וֹב בְּעֵֽינֵיכֶם֙ בְּשֵׁ֣ם הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְחִתְמ֖וּ בְּטַבַּ֣עַת הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ כִּֽי־כְתָ֞ב אֲשֶׁר־נִכְתָּ֣ב בְּשֵׁם־הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ וְנַחְתּ֛וֹם בְּטַבַּ֥עַת הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֵ֥ין לְהָשִֽׁיב׃
records.gloss: And you, write concerning the Jews as [is] good in your eyes in [the] name of the king, and seal with [the] signet ring of the king, for a writing that is written in [the] name of the king and sealed with [the] signet ring of the king, there is no turning back.
pieces: Now you write whatever you think best concerning the Jews, in the king's name, and seal it with the king's signet ring. For a decree written in the king's name and sealed with the king's ring cannot be revoked."

L.8: And you, write concerning the Jews as is good in your eyes, in the name of the king, and seal it with the signet ring of the king, for a writing that is written in the name of the king and sealed with the signet ring of the king cannot be revoked."

R.8: Now you two write whatever you think is best for the Jews. Write it in the king's name and seal it with the king's ring. No order written in the king's name and sealed with his ring can ever be canceled."

decisions.choice: you: Esther and Mordecai together
decisions.reason: The pronoun and the verb are plural. The king gives the authority to both of them.

decisions.choice: a sealed royal decree cannot be revoked
decisions.reason: The book says that the laws of Persia and Media cannot be revoked (1:19), and the same rule appears in Daniel 6. Since Haman's decree cannot be canceled, the king lets Esther and Mordecai write a second decree that will counter it.

decisions.choice: for: the reason works both ways
decisions.reason: The "for" explains why the king does not simply cancel Haman's letters, and also why the new letter will carry full force: it too will be sealed and cannot be revoked.

decisions.choice: you two
decisions.reason: Readable shows that "you" is plural, which English does not otherwise mark.

records.source: וַיִּקָּרְא֣וּ סֹפְרֵֽי־הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ בָּֽעֵת־הַ֠הִיא בַּחֹ֨דֶשׁ הַשְּׁלִישִׁ֜י הוּא־חֹ֣דֶשׁ סִיוָ֗ן בִּשְׁלוֹשָׁ֣ה וְעֶשְׂרִים֮ בּוֹ֒ וַיִּכָּתֵ֣ב כְּֽכָל־אֲשֶׁר־צִוָּ֣ה מָרְדֳּכַ֣י אֶל־הַיְּהוּדִ֡ים וְאֶ֣ל הָאֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנִֽים־וְהַפַּחוֹת֩ וְשָׂרֵ֨י הַמְּדִינ֜וֹת אֲשֶׁ֣ר׀מֵהֹ֣דּוּ וְעַד־כּ֗וּשׁ שֶׁ֣בַע וְעֶשְׂרִ֤ים וּמֵאָה֙ מְדִינָ֔ה מְדִינָ֤ה וּמְדִינָה֙ כִּכְתָבָ֔הּ וְעַ֥ם וָעָ֖ם כִּלְשֹׁנ֑וֹ וְאֶ֨ל־הַיְּהוּדִ֔ים כִּכְתָבָ֖ם וְכִלְשׁוֹנָֽם׃
records.gloss: And were called [the] scribes of the king at the time the that, in the month the third, that [is the] month Sivan, on three and twenty in it, and it was written according to all that commanded Mordecai to the Jews and to the satraps and the governors and [the] officials of the provinces that [are] from India and to Cush, seven and twenty and a hundred provinces, province and province according to its script and people and people according to its language, and to the Jews according to their script and according to their language.
pieces: So the king's scribes were summoned at that time, on the twenty-third day of the third month, the month of Sivan. Everything Mordecai ordered was written down, to the Jews and to the satraps, the governors, and the officials of the 127 provinces stretching from India to Cush. It was written to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, and to the Jews in their own script and language.

L.9: And the scribes of the king were summoned at that time, in the third month, which is the month Sivan, on the twenty-third day of it. And it was written according to all that Mordecai commanded, to the Jews and to the satraps and the governors and the officials of the provinces from India to Cush, 127 provinces, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, and to the Jews in their script and in their language.

R.9: So the king's secretaries were called in on the twenty-third day of the third month, the month of Sivan, in late spring. They wrote down everything Mordecai ordered. The letters went to the Jews, and to the regional governors, the provincial governors, and the officials of all 127 provinces from India to Cush. Each province received the letter in its own system of writing, and each people in its own language. The Jews also received it in their own writing and language.

decisions.choice: the twenty-third of Sivan: about seventy days after Haman's decree
decisions.reason: Sivan is the third month of the year, in late spring (May to June). Haman's letters were written on the thirteenth day of the first month (3:12), so the new letters come about two months and ten days later, with about nine months left before the day set for the attack (verse 12).

decisions.choice: the wording follows 3:12, with the Jews now addressed
decisions.reason: The verse repeats almost word for word how Haman's decree was written (3:12), but now it is Mordecai who commands, and the Jews themselves are among those written to, in their own script and language.

decisions.choice: satraps, governors and officials, from India to Cush
decisions.reason: Satraps ruled the large regions of the Persian empire, governors smaller provinces, and officials served under them (3:12). The empire reached from India in the east to Cush, the land south of Egypt along the upper Nile, in the west (1:1).

decisions.choice: each in its own script and language
decisions.reason: The Persian empire wrote to its many peoples in their own languages and scripts, as Haman's letters had done (1:22; 3:12).

decisions.choice: regional governors
decisions.reason: As throughout Esther, Readable says "regional governors" for the satraps; Literal and Balanced keep "satraps".

decisions.choice: in late spring
decisions.reason: Readable adds the season, since the Hebrew month name means little to most readers.

records.source: וַיִּכְתֹּ֗ב בְּשֵׁם֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֹ֔שׁ וַיַּחְתֹּ֖ם בְּטַבַּ֣עַת הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַיִּשְׁלַ֣ח סְפָרִ֡ים בְּיַד֩ הָרָצִ֨ים בַּסּוּסִ֜ים רֹכְבֵ֤י הָרֶ֨כֶשׁ֙ הָֽאֲחַשְׁתְּרָנִ֔ים בְּנֵ֖י הָֽרַמָּכִֽים׃
records.gloss: And he wrote in [the] name of the king Ahasuerus and sealed with [the] signet ring of the king, and sent letters by [the] hand of the runners on the horses, riders of the steeds, the royal [ones], sons of the mares,
pieces: Mordecai wrote in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed it with the king's signet ring, and he sent the letters by mounted couriers riding swift horses bred for the royal service,

L.10: And he wrote in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed it with the signet ring of the king, and he sent letters by the hand of the couriers on horses, riders of the royal steeds, offspring of the mares,

R.10: Mordecai wrote the letters in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed them with the king's ring. He sent them out with messengers riding fast horses from the king's own stables.

decisions.choice: he wrote: Mordecai, who gave the orders (verse 9)
decisions.reason: The subject is not named, but it is Mordecai, who now holds the king's ring (verse 2) and was told to write (verse 8).

decisions.choice: steeds, royal, sons of the mares: the fastest horses of the royal post
decisions.reason: Several of these words are rare. The word rendered "royal" is a Persian loanword whose exact meaning is not certain; "sons of the mares" seems to mean horses bred from special breeding stock. Together they describe the fastest horses kept for the king's service.

decisions.choice: couriers on horses: the Persian royal post
decisions.reason: The Persian kings kept a relay of mounted messengers with fresh horses along the royal roads, which carried orders across the empire quickly. Haman's letters were sent by couriers too (3:13, 15), but horses are mentioned only here.

decisions.choice: Mordecai
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the writer, since "he" could be read as the king.

records.source: אֲשֶׁר֩ נָתַ֨ן הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ לַיְּהוּדִ֣ים׀אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּכָל־עִיר־וָעִ֗יר לְהִקָּהֵל֮ וְלַעֲמֹ֣ד עַל־נַפְשָׁם֒ לְהַשְׁמִיד֩ וְלַהֲרֹ֨ג וּלְאַבֵּ֜ד אֶת־כָּל־חֵ֨יל עַ֧ם וּמְדִינָ֛ה הַצָּרִ֥ים אֹתָ֖ם טַ֣ף וְנָשִׁ֑ים וּשְׁלָלָ֖ם לָבֽוֹז׃
records.gloss: that had given the king to the Jews who [are] in every city and city to assemble and to stand for their life, to annihilate and to kill and to destroy every force of a people and province that attacks them, little ones and women, and their spoil to plunder,
pieces: saying that the king allowed the Jews in every city to gather and defend their lives, and to destroy, kill, and wipe out any armed force of any people or province that might attack them, together with their children and women, and to plunder their goods,

L.11: in which the king allowed the Jews who were in every city to assemble and to stand for their lives, to annihilate and to kill and to destroy every armed force of any people or province that attacks them, little ones and women, and to plunder their spoil,

R.11: The letters said that the king allowed the Jews in every city to gather together and defend themselves. If any army of any people or province attacked them, the Jews could destroy, kill, and wipe out those attackers, along with their children and women, and take their goods.

decisions.choice: the same words as Haman's decree, turned around
decisions.reason: The three verbs, "little ones and women", and "to plunder their spoil" are taken word for word from Haman's decree against the Jews (3:13). The new decree gives the Jews the same rights against those who attack them. In the event, the Jews did not lay a hand on the plunder (9:10, 15, 16).

decisions.choice: little ones and women: the attackers' families
alternatives: any force that attacks them, their children and women (the Jews' own families)
decisions.reason: The words stand without a connecting word after "every armed force ... that attacks them". Read as in 3:13, which they repeat, they name the families of the attackers. Another reading takes them with "attacks": "that attacks them, their little ones and women", so that the decree lets the Jews defend their own children and wives. The Hebrew allows both.

decisions.choice: to assemble and stand for their lives: to band together in self-defense
decisions.reason: To "stand for one's life" means to defend oneself (9:16). The permission is to resist those who attack them.

decisions.choice: every force ... that attacks them: armed attackers only
decisions.reason: The word for "force" means an army or armed band, and the participle means those who show hostility, here by attacking. The decree is aimed at those who take up arms against the Jews.

decisions.choice: saying that; The letters said that
decisions.reason: The Hebrew links this verse to the letters of verse 10 with a single relative word; Balanced and Readable say that this is what the letters contained.

records.source: בְּי֣וֹם אֶחָ֔ד בְּכָל־מְדִינ֖וֹת הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֑וֹשׁ בִּשְׁלוֹשָׁ֥ה עָשָׂ֛ר לְחֹ֥דֶשׁ שְׁנֵים־עָשָׂ֖ר הוּא־חֹ֥דֶשׁ אֲדָֽר׃
records.gloss: on day one in all [the] provinces of the king Ahasuerus, on [the] thirteenth of [the] month twelfth, that [is the] month Adar.
pieces: on a single day in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month Adar.

L.12: on one day in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, on the thirteenth of the twelfth month, which is the month Adar.

R.12: This was to be on one day in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus: the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar, in late winter.

decisions.choice: the thirteenth of Adar: the day set for the Jews' destruction
decisions.reason: This is the date chosen by lot for Haman's decree (3:7, 13). The day set for the Jews' destruction becomes the day they are allowed to defend themselves.

decisions.choice: on one day: the permission is for that day
decisions.reason: The decree gives the Jews the right to act on the one day when the attack was to come, in every province at once.

decisions.choice: in late winter
decisions.reason: Readable adds the season (February to March), as the Hebrew month name means little to most readers.

records.source: פַּתְשֶׁ֣גֶן הַכְּתָ֗ב לְהִנָּ֤תֵֽן דָּת֙ בְּכָל־מְדִינָ֣ה וּמְדִינָ֔ה גָּל֖וּי לְכָל־הָעַמִּ֑ים וְלִהְי֨וֹת הַיְּהוּדִ֤ים עֲתִידִים֙ לַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה לְהִנָּקֵ֖ם מֵאֹיְבֵיהֶֽם׃
records.gloss: [The] copy of the writing to be given [as] law in every province and province, published to all the peoples, and to be the Jews ready for the day the this to avenge themselves on their enemies.
pieces: A copy of the text was to be issued as law in every province and made known to all the peoples, so that the Jews would be ready on that day to take revenge on their enemies.

L.13: A copy of the writing was to be given as law in every province, published to all the peoples, and the Jews were to be ready for this day, to avenge themselves on their enemies.

R.13: A copy of the order was to be made law in every province and announced to all the people there. Then the Jews would be ready on that day to pay back their enemies.

decisions.choice: the wording follows 3:14
decisions.reason: The verse repeats how Haman's decree was published (3:14), so that everyone would know of the new law as they knew of the old.

decisions.choice: avenge themselves: to repay those who attack them
decisions.reason: The verb means to take vengeance, to repay a wrong done, often as a just punishment. Here it is limited by verse 11 to those who attack the Jews.

decisions.choice: ready: written and read forms differ only in spelling
decisions.reason: The written text and the form the scribes marked to be read spell the word for "ready" slightly differently. Both mean the same thing.

decisions.choice: pay back
decisions.reason: Readable uses the plain phrase "pay back" for "avenge themselves".

records.source: הָרָצִ֞ים רֹכְבֵ֤י הָרֶ֨כֶשׁ֙ הָֽאֲחַשְׁתְּרָנִ֔ים יָֽצְא֛וּ מְבֹהָלִ֥ים וּדְחוּפִ֖ים בִּדְבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וְהַדָּ֥ת נִתְּנָ֖ה בְּשׁוּשַׁ֥ן הַבִּירָֽה׃פ
records.gloss: The runners, riders of the steeds, the royal [ones], went out hastened and pressed by [the] word of the king, and the law was given in Susa the citadel.
pieces: The couriers, riding the royal horses, went out in haste, urged on by the king's command. And the decree was issued in the citadel of Susa.

L.14: The couriers, riders of the royal steeds, went out, hastened and pressed on by the word of the king. And the law was given in Susa the citadel.

R.14: The messengers rode out quickly on the king's fast horses, because the king had ordered them to hurry. The order was also announced in the royal fortress in Susa.

decisions.choice: the wording follows 3:15
decisions.reason: The couriers go out in haste and the law is issued in Susa the citadel, as with Haman's decree (3:15). There the city of Susa was thrown into confusion; here it will rejoice (verse 15).

decisions.choice: hastened and pressed: driven to hurry
decisions.reason: The two verbs both mean being hurried along; the second is the verb used of Haman hurrying home in 6:12.

decisions.choice: Susa the citadel; the citadel of Susa; the royal fortress in Susa
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for the royal fortress at Susa.

records.source: וּמָרְדֳּכַ֞י יָצָ֣א׀מִלִּפְנֵ֣י הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ בִּלְב֤וּשׁ מַלְכוּת֙ תְּכֵ֣לֶת וָח֔וּר וַעֲטֶ֤רֶת זָהָב֙ גְּדוֹלָ֔ה וְתַכְרִ֥יךְ בּ֖וּץ וְאַרְגָּמָ֑ן וְהָעִ֣יר שׁוּשָׁ֔ן צָהֲלָ֖ה וְשָׂמֵֽחָה׃
records.gloss: And Mordecai went out from before the king in clothing of royalty, violet and white, and a crown of gold great, and a mantle of fine linen and purple. And the city Susa shouted and rejoiced.
pieces: Mordecai left the king's presence wearing royal robes of blue and white, a large gold crown, and a cloak of fine linen and purple. And the city of Susa shouted for joy.

L.15: And Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal clothing of blue and white, and with a great crown of gold, and a mantle of fine linen and purple. And the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced.

R.15: Mordecai left the king wearing royal clothes of blue and white, a large gold crown, and a purple robe of fine linen. And the people of Susa shouted and celebrated.

decisions.choice: blue, white and purple: royal colors
decisions.reason: Blue-violet and white were the colors of the hangings in the king's palace (1:6), and purple dye was costly and worn by royalty. Mordecai is dressed as one of the highest men of the kingdom.

decisions.choice: a great crown of gold: a large golden headdress, not the king's crown
decisions.reason: The word here is not the one used for the royal crown (6:8) but a general word for a crown or wreath. It marks Mordecai's high office.

decisions.choice: the city shouted and rejoiced: the reverse of 3:15
decisions.reason: When Haman's decree went out, "the city of Susa was confused" (3:15), and Mordecai went out in sackcloth crying aloud (4:1). Now he goes out in royal clothes, and the city shouts for joy.

decisions.choice: blue
decisions.reason: The color named is a blue-violet; "blue" is the closest plain English word.

decisions.choice: the people of Susa
decisions.reason: Readable says "the people" for "the city", which means its inhabitants.

records.heading: Light and gladness for the Jews

records.source: לַיְּהוּדִ֕ים הָֽיְתָ֥ה אוֹרָ֖ה וְשִׂמְחָ֑ה וְשָׂשֹׂ֖ן וִיקָֽר׃
records.gloss: For the Jews there was light and gladness and joy and honor.
pieces: For the Jews it was a time of light and gladness, joy and honor.

L.16: For the Jews there was light and gladness and joy and honor.

R.16: For the Jews it was like light after darkness: a time of gladness, joy, and honor.

decisions.choice: light: well-being and happiness
decisions.reason: "Light" stands for prosperity, safety and gladness, after a time of darkness and danger (Psalm 97:11; Proverbs 13:9).

decisions.choice: gladness, joy and honor after mourning
decisions.reason: When the decree against them was first known, there was "great mourning among the Jews, with fasting and weeping and wailing" (4:3). Now four words of joy answer it. "Honor" is the word Haman sought for himself in chapter 6.

decisions.choice: like light after darkness
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of light by its contrast with the dark days before.

records.source: וּבְכָל־מְדִינָ֨ה וּמְדִינָ֜ה וּבְכָל־עִ֣יר וָעִ֗יר מְקוֹם֙ אֲשֶׁ֨ר דְּבַר־הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ וְדָתוֹ֙ מַגִּ֔יעַ שִׂמְחָ֤ה וְשָׂשׂוֹן֙ לַיְּהוּדִ֔ים מִשְׁתֶּ֖ה וְי֣וֹם ט֑וֹב וְרַבִּ֞ים מֵֽעַמֵּ֤י הָאָ֨רֶץ֙ מִֽתְיַהֲדִ֔ים כִּֽי־נָפַ֥ל פַּֽחַד־הַיְּהוּדִ֖ים עֲלֵיהֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And in every province and province, and in every city and city, [the] place where [the] word of the king and his law [was] reaching, gladness and joy for the Jews, a feast and a good day. And many from [the] peoples of the land were becoming Jews, for had fallen [the] dread of the Jews on them.
pieces: In every province and in every city, wherever the king's command and his decree arrived, there was gladness and joy among the Jews, with feasting and a holiday. And many people of the land became Jews, because fear of the Jews had come over them.

L.17: And in every province and in every city, wherever the word of the king and his law reached, there was gladness and joy for the Jews, a feast and a good day. And many from the peoples of the land became Jews, for the dread of the Jews had fallen on them.

R.17: In every province and every city where the king's order arrived, the Jews were glad and full of joy. They held feasts and had a holiday. Many people of other nations in the land became Jews, because they had become afraid of the Jews.

decisions.choice: became Jews: joined the Jewish people
decisions.reason: The verb is found only here in the Bible. Formed from the word "Jew", it most likely means that people joined the Jews, taking up their way of life. It could also mean that they claimed to be Jews or took the Jews' side without truly joining them, out of fear.

decisions.choice: a feast and a good day: a holiday of feasting
decisions.reason: A "good day" is a day of celebration, a holiday (9:19, 22; 1 Samuel 25:8). This celebration looks ahead to the feast of Purim (9:17-22).

decisions.choice: the dread of the Jews: fear of the Jews
decisions.reason: The phrase means the fear that people felt toward the Jews, not fear that the Jews felt. The same is said in 9:2.

decisions.choice: a holiday
decisions.reason: "A good day" is a holiday; Balanced and Readable say so.
